specPoints.text: understand how elements are arranged in the Periodic Table: in order of atomic number, in groups and periods

primer.text: The atomic number you met in Atomic Structure is the key that unlocks the periodic table: it counts an atom's protons and labels every element uniquely. This note shows how the table orders elements by that number, and how its rows and columns encode electron shells and outer electrons. If atomic number still feels new, revisit Atomic Structure before starting.

lessons.title: In Order of Atomic Number
lessons.opening: The periodic table lists every element in order of increasing atomic number, so each element takes one step up in protons from its neighbour. That single ordering rule quietly does clever work: elements with similar properties land in the same column. The atomic number is also each element's fingerprint - electrons shift during reactions, but that number never does.
keyPoints: Over 100 elements have been isolated and identified so far.
Elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic number.
Each element carries one proton more than the element before it.
Ordering by atomic number places elements with similar properties in the same columns.
An element's atomic number is its fingerprint: it never changes, even in reactions.

low.restatement: Read the table left to right and the proton count climbs by one at every step; that ordering is what gathers elements with similar properties into the same column.
low.analogy: It is like a numbered queue: everyone joins exactly one place further along, and the numbering is arranged so that people with the same interests end up standing together in the same line.
low.examPointer: The fingerprint line earns easy marks: electrons come and go in reactions, but the atomic number of an element never changes.

medium.restatement: Over 100 identified elements are laid out in order of increasing atomic number, each one proton more than the element before. The ordering is chosen so that elements with similar properties finish up in the same vertical column - and the atomic number is unique to each element, never altered by chemical reactions.
medium.analogy: Think of a stadium where every seat number increases by exactly one along the row: the strict numbering is what lets supporters of the same team find each other.
medium.examPointer: Two facts travel together in exam answers: the order is by atomic number, and that number is the element's fingerprint which no reaction can rewrite.

check.stem: What runs along the modern periodic table's left-to-right order?

options.explanation: Every step along the table adds one proton, which is what atomic number counts.
Mass-based ordering was the older idea; the modern table follows proton count.
Discovery order would scatter similar elements; the table orders by structure.
Names are labels, not the organising principle.

check.stem: How does an element's proton count compare with its left-hand neighbour's?

options.explanation: Adjacent elements differ by a single proton, which is why the order is so regular.
Eight is a period-length idea, not the neighbour-to-neighbour step.
Doubling would tear through the sequence; the step is one.
The pattern is as fixed as it gets: plus one every step.

check.stem: Why is the table ordered by atomic number rather than by something else?

options.text: So that elements with similar properties end up in the same columns
options.explanation: The arrangement is functional: chemical families gather vertically.

options.text: Because atomic numbers are easier to spell
options.explanation: The choice is chemical, not cosmetic.

options.text: Because proton counts can change during reactions
options.explanation: Proton counts are fixed; that stability is precisely why they can anchor the table.

options.text: So the table fits neatly on one page
options.explanation: Page layout has nothing to do with it; property patterns do.

check.stem: In a reaction an atom gains electrons. Which number is unchanged?

options.explanation: Electron changes cannot touch the proton count, so the element keeps its identity.
That is exactly what changed when the electron was gained.
Gaining an electron alters the charge by definition.

options.text: None - gaining an electron makes a new element
options.explanation: Only a change in proton count makes a new element; electrons merely make ions.

check.stem: Where do elements with similar chemical properties end up in the table?

options.explanation: Similar properties sharing a column is the payoff of the atomic-number ordering.
Rows collect neighbours in proton count, not chemical look-alikes.
No diagonal rule governs the basic arrangement.
The whole design exists to keep chemical families together.

lessons.title: Groups and Periods
lessons.opening: Every line on the periodic table carries meaning. Periods count electron shells and groups count outer-shell electrons, with the last column named Group 0. Read an element's position and you can state both counts at a glance.
keyPoints: Vertical columns are groups; horizontal rows are periods.
The period number gives the number of electron shells an atom holds.
The group number gives the number of electrons in the outermost shell.
Groups run 1 to 7, with the final column named Group 0 instead of 8.
A Period 2 element has two shells; a Group 6 element has six outer electrons.

low.restatement: Rows are periods and count an atom's electron shells; columns are groups and count its outer-shell electrons, so the two numbers together place any atom exactly. Groups run 1 to 7, then a final column called Group 0.
low.analogy: The table works like a hotel: the floor number tells how many storeys of electrons the atom has, and the room number along the corridor tells who is at the door - the outer electrons.
low.examPointer: Read the two numbers straight off the element's position: period 3, group 5 means three shells and five outer electrons.

medium.restatement: Periods are the horizontal rows, numbered 1 to 7, and a period number is the count of electron shells - Period 2 atoms have two shells. Groups are the vertical columns, numbered 1 to 7 with a final Group 0, and a group number is the count of outer-shell electrons - Group 6 atoms hold six electrons in their outermost shell.
medium.analogy: Think of the table as a block of flats: the period is the floor plan (how many storeys of electrons), while the group is the street-facing room number (how many electrons stand at the outer door, ready to react).
medium.examPointer: Position questions want both numbers read and translated: shells from the period, outer electrons from the group - and Group 0 is the given name of the last column, not a count of nothing.

check.stem: Which description matches the table's rows and columns?

options.text: Periods are rows; groups are columns
options.explanation: The vocabulary is fixed: periods across, groups down.

options.text: Periods are columns; groups are rows
options.explanation: The two names are swapped; remember groups go down like gravity.

options.text: Both rows and columns are called groups
options.explanation: Only the vertical columns carry the name group.

options.text: Neither direction has a special name
options.explanation: Both directions are named because both carry information.

check.stem: What does the period number tell you about an atom?

options.text: How many shells of electrons it holds
options.explanation: Period 3 atoms have three shells; the row number is the shell count.

options.text: How many electrons are in the outer shell
options.explanation: That is the group number's job, not the period's.
Proton count is the atomic number, read from order rather than position name.
Neutrons vary between isotopes and appear nowhere in the position numbers.

check.stem: What does the group number tell you about an atom?

options.text: How many electrons sit in its outermost shell
options.explanation: Group 4 atoms carry four outer electrons; the column is the outer count.
Shell count comes from the period row, not the group column.

options.text: How many isotopes the element has
options.explanation: Isotope counts are properties of samples and discovery, not of position.
Atomic mass is a separate number printed in the element's box.

check.stem: Which numbering does the table use for its columns?

options.text: 1 to 7, then a final column called Group 0
options.explanation: The last column is named 0 instead of 8 - a naming convention of the table.
The leftmost column is Group 1; the 0 belongs to the far right.
The final column deliberately breaks the run and is called Group 0.
This course numbers the groups; letters belong to other table styles.

check.stem: An atom has 3 shells and 5 electrons in its outermost. Where does it sit?

options.explanation: Shell count sets the period, outer-electron count sets the group.
The two translations are swapped; shells give the period.
Group 0 is the last column's name, not a home for five outer electrons.
Periods run only 1 to 7; three shells means Period 3.

glossary.definition: The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom.
A vertical column of the periodic table, numbering the electrons in the outermost shell.
A horizontal row of the periodic table, numbering the shells of electrons an atom holds.
One of the layers, or orbital paths, around the nucleus where electrons are found.
The electrons in the outermost shell, counted by the group number.
The final column of the table, named 0 instead of 8.
